newsitem.title: UK: Wirral South voters offer Major little hope.
newsitem.headline: Wirral South voters offer Major little hope.

text.p: Voters on England's prosperous Wirral peninsula on Friday offered the ruling Conservatives little hope of reversing their crushing by-election defeat in national elections due by May.

Labour on Thursday seized the Wirral South constituency the Conservatives had held with ease since it was created in 1983, boding ill for the ruling party's chances of winning an unprecedented fifth term of office in the general election.
Labour's Ben Chapman overturned a Conservative majority of 8,183 votes to win by a margin of 7,888 votes in the by-election caused by the death of Barry Porter.
The Conservatives took some comfort from the fact they have often lost seats in by-elections during their 18 years in power, only to win them back at national elections.
But many voters in Wirral South, a natural Conservative territory of wealthy villages and suburban housing estates, said they had no intention of switching back.
"I voted Labour for the first time in my life and will vote the same way next time," said a smartly-dressed middle-aged woman.

She said her four daughters had university degrees but had been unable to find full-time work and her husband had lost his job in shipbuilding, the Wirral's biggest industry until it was closed down in the late 1980s.
A young woman with a small baby said she had not voted in the past four elections, but had backed Labour on Thursday.
"We made a conscious decision to vote this time, my husband and I. It's time something was done," she said.

Interior minister Michael Howard, visiting the constituency on the morning after the poll, shrugged off what he called "a disappointing result" and said he was confident the Conservatives would win the seat back.
But if one young couple who voted Conservative on Thursday are representative, Major must do much more to win back voters.
Neil Francis and Lynn Thomas, who run a small business in the town of Heswall, said they might vote Labour next time.
"It depends on whether John Major bucks his ideas up," said Francis. "I want to see things like unemployment and Europe sorted out."

Another young woman said Labour's heavy-hitting campaign had persuaded her to vote. She had been telephoned several times in the past few weeks and on the day of the poll. "I was hounded into it, but I will vote Labour next time too," she said.
Labour devoted heavy resources to its campaign, run from a high-tech office manned by dozens of officials and volunteers.
Barely a day passed without a visit by a top party figure. Labour leader Tony Blair went to the constituency three times.

Blair is credited with finally making Labour appear electable after 18 years of Conservative rule by pushing the historically left-wing party firmly into the centre. The party now consistently leads the Conservaties by 20 points in polls.

The winning candidate Chapman typifies Blair's new Labour. A prominent local businessman who lives in a handsome sandstone cottage in an exclusive part of Heswall, he is guaranteed not to alarm former Conservative voters who fear Labour remaims tied to the unions.

Emerging bleary-eyed on Friday after a late night victory party, Chapman said: "This is not just a by-election effect, this is a permanent view, its a change of heart they (the voters) are coming to Labour."
